y-m-58-09.title: Wetin we fit read from delivery-fee table
y-m-58-09.topic: Function correspondence: fee set by interval
y-m-58-09.goal: From fee table (correspondence wey value set by interval), judge what rule needed to settle fee at boundary value; assume one rule and find weight pairs wey follow condition; explain why some intervals get no answer.
y-m-58-09.material: This na made-up delivery-company fee table. Weight unit kg, fee unit 원, and weight above 0 but at most 10 kg. 0 to 1 kg interval: 3000원; 1 to 2 kg: 3500원; 2 to 5 kg: 4500원; 5 to 10 kg: 6000원. Dem no separately explain interval boundaries (1, 2, 5 kg).

y-m-58-09.s.s1.prompt: To know fee for box wey weigh exactly 2 kg, wetin else we need?
y-m-58-09.s.s1.hint.0: Find every table interval wey 2 kg fit belong to.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think wetin problem fit happen if one weight get two different fees.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.o.a: Sum of box width, length, and height
y-m-58-09.s.s1.r.a: You decide say extra information needed even though fee table depend only on weight.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.o.b: Rule wey decide which interval boundary value belong to
y-m-58-09.s.s1.r.b: This judgment notice say boundary value belong to both intervals.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.o.c: Weight no dey fee table, so no fee fit decide. More information no go help.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.r.c: You no see say 2 kg dey in table as end of an interval.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.o.d: Set fee as average of 3500원 and 4500원.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.r.d: You fill unclear part with calculation wey get no basis.
y-m-58-09.s.s1.explain: 2 kg fit belong either to 1-to-2 kg interval or 2-to-5 kg interval. Only if one rule say like 'boundary belongs to lower interval (up to and including)' one fee become fixed; only then this be function (exactly one fee for each weight).
y-m-58-09.s.s2.prompt: Assume notice say 'upper-end weight of every interval included in that interval (1 kg=3000원, 2 kg=3500원, 5 kg=4500원, 10 kg=6000원)'. Enter 2 pairs of boxes w1, w2 (kg), where second box weigh at least 2 times first but same fee (w2≤10); both weights above 0 and pairs dey in different intervals.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write lightest and heaviest weight in one interval and test whether doubled weight still dey in that interval.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.hint.1: Do same test for every interval and mark which intervals possible or impossible.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.fail.c1: Weight gats be above 0, and w2 gats be 10 or less.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.ok.c2: Second weight at least 2 times first.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.fail.c2: Second weight gats be at least 2 times first.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.explain: 0.4 kg and 0.8 kg both cost 3000원; 2.2 kg and 4.5 kg both 4500원. Pairs gats use different fee intervals to count as different (even if you make more pairs in same interval, count them as same case). Only intervals wey fit this condition na 3000원 and 4500원.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.prompt: In 1-to-2 kg interval (3500원) and 5-to-10 kg interval (6000원), explain in one or two sentences why no pair dey.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Choose weight above 1 kg, double am and check which interval e enter.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether doubling weight above 5 kg still dey inside table range.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You explain both places, 1-to-2 kg interval and 5-to-10 kg interval?
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You check with numbers 'where e go when doubled'?
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.model.0: Double any weight above 1 kg, e go pass 2 kg into next interval (4500원). So no doubled pair dey within 3500원 interval. If weight above 5 kg, doubling am pass 10 kg and leave the table range, so 6000원 interval no get pair too.
y-m-58-09.s.s2.because.model.1: For 3500원 interval, doubling weight pass 2 kg, so fee change. For 6000원 interval, doubling am pass 10 kg, beyond table range.

y-m-58-02.title: Wetin walking record fit tell us
y-m-58-02.goal: From distances measured at set times, know between-times movement na guess only; adjust judgment as data grow and distinguish average from interval speed.
y-m-58-02.material: This na made-up record of Jisu walking home to school 1000 m away. Departure na 0 min; every 2 min measure distance from home (m). Data reveal gradually. We no know if she ever walk back toward home.
y-m-58-02.thinking.2: Compare mean speed and interval speed
y-m-58-02.prereq.0: Speed = distance traveled ÷ time taken (middle school)
y-m-58-02.s.s1.prompt: Write judgment each time data increase.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.hint.1: For between-times, separate known fact from guess.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.info: 0 min: 0 m, 2 min: 200 m, 4 min: 400 m.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: About where Jisu go be from home after 10 min?
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.after: b predict if speed stay same; c carefully say outside data unknown. Both reasonable with this data.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You assume she stop at 4-minute position.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Around 1000 m if she keep same speed
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This conditional prediction continue given rate (200 m each 2 min).
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Data now no decide what happen after

y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now with data up to here, what can you say about after 10 min?
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Same values at 6 and 8 mean same position then. 10-minute value not known yet, so flat claim (a) no evidence.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 400 m or farther if she no turn back
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This reflect new data but make no-return a condition.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Can't decide whether she start walking or go back
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: What happens after measured times no dey data.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What best thing to say about Jisu from 6 to 8 min?
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Even with more data, 6-8 min interval never measured. You fit guess she rest, but no state as fact.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Measurements same at 2-min interval, so assert she stay one place whole 2 min
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read same endpoints as same all along between them.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Only confirmed she same place at 6 and 8; movement between unknown from this data
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This separates measured times from in-between actions.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Speed from 6 to 8 was constant 100 m/min
y-m-58-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You carry earlier interval speed into this one.
y-m-58-02.s.s1.reflect: At first b and c both reasonable. As data grow, boundary between known and guessed clear. You need not reverse judgment; changing confidence is also revision.
y-m-58-02.s.s2.prompt: Find overall average speed over 12 min and interval speed from 8 to 12, compare; explain difference in 1-2 sentences.
y-m-58-02.s.s2.hint.0: Speed = distance/time. First choose which two times' values to use.
y-m-58-02.s.s2.hint.1: Find positions at 8 and 12 min in table; calculate difference.
y-m-58-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Your speeds show units (m/min) and time interval clearly?
y-m-58-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Use data (e.g. stop time) explain why average and interval speeds differ?
y-m-58-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Separate 'she rested' as confirmed fact or guess?
y-m-58-02.s.s2.model.0: Overall average =1000÷12≈83 m/min. From 400m at 8 min to 1000m at 12, traveled 600m in 4min: 600÷4=150m/min. Little movement in between lowers average, so interval speed higher.
y-m-58-02.s.s2.model.1: Average ≈83m/min (1000÷12); interval 8-12 is 150m/min (600÷4). She seems barely move between 6-8, lowering whole-trip average.
y-m-58-02.s.s2.model.2: 12-min average ≈83m/min; 8-12 interval 150m/min. Maybe she stayed still between 6 and 8, lowering overall average.

y-m-58-03.title: Conditions for trusting building-height estimate from shadows
y-m-58-03.topic: Similarity: assumptions behind height estimate from shadows
y-m-58-03.goal: Judge assumptions needed for shadow-based height method; say direction error goes when assumption fail; suggest needed extra measurement.
y-m-58-03.material: Harin measure pole height 1.2m, pole shadow 1.8m; same day building shadow 27m. Shadow means base to shadow tip. If sunlight angle with ground is θ, height/shadow=tanθ. Harin estimate building height with this ratio.
y-m-58-03.thinking.0: Separate required conditions from irrelevant info
y-m-58-03.thinking.1: Reason direction result shift if assumption breaks
y-m-58-03.prereq.3: Note H3 only task difficulty/support, no grade assignment. Assume high-school Basic Math 2 after middle-school basics of functions, figures, data.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose every condition absolutely needed for trustworthy building estimate.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write how to find tanθ for pole-shadow-sun triangle and building-shadow-sun triangle.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write what must match for θ equal at both places; check whether each option affect it.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.r.a: If sun angle same and ground flat, distance no matter. This adds condition not directly related to measured values.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.o.b: Pole and building both perpendicular to ground
y-m-58-03.s.s1.r.b: This recalls similar triangles need equal angles.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.o.c: Pole height whole-number fraction of building height
y-m-58-03.s.s1.r.c: Maybe you think ratio must be whole number. Does ratio need integer?
y-m-58-03.s.s1.o.d: Pole and building shadows measured same time
y-m-58-03.s.s1.r.d: Sunlight-ground angle must same; this recalls it.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.r.e: If ground slant, shadow length can change.
y-m-58-03.s.s1.explain: For θ same in two right triangles, measure at same time, pole/building vertical, ground flat so shadow length is base. Then tanθ=1.2÷1.8=2/3 both places; height=27×2/3=18m. Distance and integer-multiple relation unnecessary.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.prompt: If all conditions hold, building about 18m. But shadow tip hit next building wall, and 27m measures ground only to wall bottom. Actual height compared to 18m?
y-m-58-03.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine no wall; draw where shadow tip would land on ground.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare direction (shadow length)×tanθ change as shadow longer.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.r.a: You think wall cutting shadow short mean height lower.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.r.b: Without wall, shadow would extend farther along ground.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.r.c: You ignore shadow climbing wall and use ground length as full shadow.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.o.d: If wall there, no info possible
y-m-58-03.s.s2.r.d: Even without exact value, direction can be known.
y-m-58-03.s.s2.explain: Without wall shadow goes farther on ground, so actual ground shadow >27m. Height=shadow length×tanθ; tanθ same, so height >18m. Exact unknown, but at least 18m.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.prompt: In 1-2 sentences say what else measure to get more accurate building height without wall effect and why needed.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think what info shadow tip on wall tells you.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.hint.1: Sunlight same slope; what length can you estimate if measure one more height/distance?
y-m-58-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Explain how your measurement gives ground-shadow length (or building height)?
y-m-58-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Think another method when direct measure hard (e.g. another day in open place)?
y-m-58-03.s.s3.model.0: Measure height above ground where shadow reaches wall. Sunlight must travel that much farther down to ground, so add it to get actual shadow length. Need that height for this reason.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.model.1: Could measure building shadow again in open no-wall place; without height of part climbing wall, cannot know amount cut off.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.model.2: Measure again when shadow no reach wall. Then it no fall on wall, so accurate.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.model.3: Measure again in open place or when shadow no hit wall, then compare.
y-m-58-03.s.s3.model.4: Measure angle of elevation to top from away and distance to building; trigonometric ratio give height, unaffected by wall.

y-m-58-04.title: Check report claiming mean 24 thousand 원
y-m-58-04.topic: Data representative values: using mean, median, mode
y-m-58-04.goal: For data with huge value, distinguish what mean/median/mode tell; make case where mean below median and explain.
y-m-58-04.material: Made-up monthly allowance (thousand 원) for 9 students: 10,12,12,15,15,16,18,20,100. Student reporter wrote report. Figures: 9 10 12 12 15 15 16 18 20 100.
y-m-58-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose reporter line that interprets data wrongly.
y-m-58-04.s.s1.hint.1: How many need values near mean for 'most' to be true?
y-m-58-04.s.s1.line.0: Sum of 9 data is 218, mean≈24.2 thousand 원.

y-m-58-04.s.s2.prompt: Now test scores: make 2 different sets of 5 students' integer scores 0-100, all distinct, sorted, where median≥80 and mean≥60 but below median.

y-m-58-04.s.s2.explain: Example 40,70,80,90,95: median 80, mean 75. 55,65,85,90,95: median 85, mean 78. Low scores pull mean down, while median only depends on order and stays middle value. Figures: 40 70 80 90 95 80 75 55 65 85 90 95 85 78.
y-m-58-04.s.s2.because.prompt: In 1-2 sentences explain with your example why this data mean below median.

y-m-58-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check which shifts more if lowest score change to high score.

y-m-58-04.s.s2.because.model.1: Mean come from adding all values, so one low score fit affect am plenty. Median na middle value when dem arrange am, so e hardly change even if extreme values dey, and na why mean come smaller.

y-m-58-05.title: Sum of two dice: compare two models
y-m-58-05.goal: Find how two models describing same thing differ, test both with simulation data, and explain why 'number of possible outcomes' no mean equal chance.
y-m-58-05.material: You want to know the sum of two fair dice rolled together, from 2 to 12. Two students explain. Minjun: 'The sums can be 2, 3, ..., 12, making 11 possibilities, so each is equally likely.' Seoa: 'Tell the dice apart; all 36 ordered pairs (first number, second number) are equally likely, and count the pairs for each sum.'
y-m-58-05.thinking.0: Compare the values predicted by the two models
y-m-58-05.prereq.0: List possible dice outcomes as ordered pairs (middle-school level)
y-m-58-05.prereq.1: Estimate with ratios and expected values (total trials × ratio)
y-m-58-05.s.s1.prompt: Before seeing experiment results, what is the best judgment about the two explanations?
y-m-58-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write all ordered pairs whose sum is 2 and whose sum is 7.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the explanations give different predictions for sums 2 and 7.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.o.a: Minjun is right. There are only 11 possible sums, so they are all equally likely
y-m-58-05.s.s1.r.a: You only counted the possible outcomes; you did not consider how often each happens.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.o.b: Both explanations predict the same for each sum, so there is no need to compare them
y-m-58-05.s.s1.r.b: Maybe you have not actually calculated what each explanation predicts for each sum.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.o.c: Seoa's explanation is more convincing because each sum has a different number of cases
y-m-58-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment examines how many ordered pairs make each sum.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.o.d: We no fit know which one correct without experiment.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.r.d: This careful judgment separate checking structure from experimenting and choose how to check.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.explain: Sum 2 has only one case, (1,1), but sum 7 has six: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). Minjun treated each sum as equally likely, but the cases are not equally likely.
y-m-58-05.s.s1.acc.0: Wanting to check by experiment is valid. But first you can see from the structure alone that each sum has a different number of cases.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.prompt: These are made-up results from a computer simulating 600 rolls. Sum 7 appeared 101 times and sum 2 appeared 15 times. Minjun predicts about 55 times each (600÷11); Seoa predicts about 100 for sum 7 and 17 for sum 2. How would you interpret this?
y-m-58-05.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate the difference between each explanation's predicted count and the actual 101.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.hint.1: Also compare the result for sum 2 to judge whether the difference is a small fluctuation or a big departure.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.o.a: It is close to Seoa's explanation. Sum 7 is much higher than Minjun's prediction
y-m-58-05.s.s2.r.a: This judgment compare distance between each model prediction and actual count.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.o.b: Minjun's explanation is possible too. 101 may be a value that came up by chance
y-m-58-05.s.s2.r.b: You may not have considered that with 600 rolls, the count would not usually depart far from around 55.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.o.c: I think 600 too small to judge either way.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.r.c: You put off judging because there were few rolls. You can examine how much difference chance could explain.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.o.d: Both explanations are wrong. They are not exactly the expected counts, so they do not fit
y-m-58-05.s.s2.r.d: You missed that an expected value is a rough target and the actual count naturally fluctuates some.
y-m-58-05.s.s2.explain: With Minjun's model, in 600 rolls sum 7 is around 55 times, and the usual chance fluctuation is within about ±14 (twice the standard deviation, about 7). 101 is much farther away, so it is hard to explain by chance. It is close to Seoa's expected 100.
y-m-58-05.s.s3.prompt: In 1 or 2 sentences, say what is wrong in Minjun's idea and about how many times out of 600 sum 6 would appear according to Seoa.
y-m-58-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write all ordered pairs with sum 6 and count them.
y-m-58-05.s.s3.hint.1: Apply the share of the 36 possible cases to the 600 rolls.
y-m-58-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You counted all ordered pairs for sum 6 and showed the calculation steps?
y-m-58-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You used sums 2 and 7 to explain why the same number of sums does not mean they are equally likely?
y-m-58-05.s.s3.model.0: Minjun said the 11 sums are equally likely, but the number of cases for each sum differs. Sum 6 has 5 cases, so its chance is 5/36 and it appears about 83 times in 600 rolls.
y-m-58-05.s.s3.model.1: Sum 2 has 1 case and sum 7 has 6; ordered-pair counts differ, which Minjun ignored. In Seoa's method, sum 6 has 5 of 36, so 600×5/36 is about 83 times.

y-m-58-06.prereq.2: ※ 'H3' na only mark for difficulty and support level of this task set; e no mean Ministry of Education assign this subject to one grade. Here, we assume high-school 'Basic Mathematics 2' stage after learning basic function meaning, geometry and data in middle-school maths.
y-m-58-06.title: If angles are equal, are figures similar? Triangles and quadrilaterals
y-m-58-06.goal: Use a counterexample to show that 'equal angles mean similar' works for triangles but not quadrilaterals, and explain the difference.
y-m-58-06.material: Doyun summarized: 'Two figures with all corresponding angles equal are similar.' The teacher asked whether it is true for every figure.
y-m-58-06.thinking.0: Separate claims that hold from claims that do not
y-m-58-06.prereq.0: Meaning of similarity (corresponding angles equal and ratios of corresponding sides equal)
y-m-58-06.s.s1.hint.0: Draw one pair of figures yourself that fits each claim.
y-m-58-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether you can satisfy a claim with figures of different shapes.
y-m-58-06.s.s1.o.a: If the four corresponding angles of two quadrilaterals are equal, the quadrilaterals are similar
y-m-58-06.s.s1.r.a: You applied the triangle rule 'equal angles mean similar' directly to quadrilaterals.
y-m-58-06.s.s1.o.b: If one side length and one angle are equal in two triangles, the triangles are congruent
y-m-58-06.s.s1.r.b: You judged that the information is enough for congruence.
y-m-58-06.s.s1.o.c: If two angles in two triangles are equal, the triangles are similar
y-m-58-06.s.s1.r.c: This recalls that a triangle's interior angle sum is fixed.
y-m-58-06.s.s1.o.d: If two triangles have equal areas, they are congruent
y-m-58-06.s.s1.r.d: You assumed that equal areas mean equal shapes.
y-m-58-06.s.s1.explain: If two angles in triangles are equal, the third angle is equal too because it is 180° minus those; that fixes the shape. (a) has a rectangle counterexample, and for (b) and (d) you can make triangles meeting the condition but with different shapes.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.prompt: Make a counterexample to (a): enter two non-similar rectangles, width w1 and height h1, width w2 and height h2 (natural lengths no more than 20). Enter two pairs with different shapes. Figures: 20 2.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.hint.0: All rectangle angles are right angles, so the angle condition already holds. Choose side lengths only.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the long-side:short-side ratios of the two rectangles.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.ok.c1: Lengths are natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Lengths must be natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The long-side:short-side ratios differ, so they are not similar.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The long-side:short-side ratios are the same, so they are similar.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.explain: 2×3 and 2×5 rectangles both have four right angles, but their long:short ratios are 3:2 and 5:2, so they are not similar. 4×4 and 3×6 have the same ratio. A pair with rectangles swapped or width and height swapped counts as the same pair.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.prompt: In 1 or 2 sentences, explain why two equal angles make triangles similar but four equal quadrilateral angles may not make them similar.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write what stays the same and what changes when a rectangle's width gets longer.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: When all triangle angles are fixed, can the side ratios still change?
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation say whether fixed angles fix the side ratios?
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you directly mention the rectangle counterexample?
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.model.0: In a triangle, fixed angles also fix side ratios, so the shape is fixed. In a quadrilateral, all angles can stay equal like a rectangle while the width:height ratio changes freely, so its shape changes.
y-m-58-06.s.s2.because.model.1: In a triangle, if two angles are equal then the third is equal too, so side ratios are equal. In a quadrilateral, even four right angles can have different side ratios, like 2×3 and 2×5.

y-m-58-10.title: Study time and scores: how far we fit go with what we say?
y-m-58-10.topic: Correlation in data: separate relationship from cause
y-m-58-10.goal: Know say seeing relation (tendency) between two variables no allow you claim cause; adjust confidence when data added, then suggest survey setup to test cause.
y-m-58-10.material: One class students were surveyed about hours studied in week before test and test scores (made-up data). Dem go reveal data step by step. Claim: 'If you increase study time, score go rise.'
y-m-58-10.thinking.0: Separate wetin data show from wetin no show
y-m-58-10.thinking.1: Adjust confidence when new information come
y-m-58-10.prereq.0: Meaning of positive and negative correlation in scatter plot
y-m-58-10.prereq.1: Read relation between two variables from table
y-m-58-10.s.s1.prompt: Write your judgment as data dey reveal.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.hint.0: Separately write whether data shown at this step confirm 'both change together' or evidence say 'one change the other'.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.hint.1: Mark whether new information support the claim, weaken am, or make another explanation possible.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.info: (Study time, score) for 6 students: (1, 45), (2, 50), (3, 58), (4, 62), (5, 70), (6, 75). Points nearly form straight line (correlation coefficient around 0.997).
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin we fit say from this data?
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.after: The 6 points nearly dey on line, so data support statement say 'tendency clear'. But word 'raises' claim cause, and data alone never decide that.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Among these 6 students, those wey study more tend to get clearly higher scores.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment state observed tendency separately from cause.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We fit be sure say study time raise score.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You treat changing together as cause.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You no notice or ignore the clear tendency.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.info: After more investigation, among these 6 students, top 3 students in earlier diagnostic test na the ones wey study 4, 5, and 6 hours.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how claim 'study time raises scores' look?
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.after: Original ability fit affect both study time and score. This no be evidence say study time get 'no' effect either. For now, best judgment na to hold off deciding.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: E still prove am, because correlation very high: 0.997.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You use correlation size as evidence for cause.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Another factor, original ability, fit explain am, so cause hard to claim.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You consider another factor wey fit affect result.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Na ability cause am, so study time no affect scores at all.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You jump from fact say another factor dey to opposite conclusion.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.info: Two more students added: (7 hours, 52 points) and (8 hours, 55 points). For all 8 students, correlation coefficient drop to around 0.40.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: How you go take this new data into account?
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.after: With 8 students, correlation weaken to 0.40 but still above 0. E suitable to change first description 'clear' to 'weak positive tendency'.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Trend still point upper-right, but e much weaker than before.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You judge strength of tendency again with the new data included.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The two new students strange, so ignore dem.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You leave out data wey no support you without reason.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Tendency disappear; actually longer study time mean lower score.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You claim opposite tendency based on only two points.
y-m-58-10.s.s1.reflect: First judgment na 'tendency dey'; second, confidence about cause reduce; third, strength of tendency too change. Notice say you no reverse first judgment, but narrow wetin you fit say.
y-m-58-10.s.s2.prompt: In 2 or 3 sentences, describe how you go design survey to check whether 'if study time increase, score go rise' be cause.
y-m-58-10.s.s2.hint.0: For this survey, students choose their own study time. Think who suppose set the time and how, so other factors affect result less.
y-m-58-10.s.s2.hint.1: Think of way to compare students with similar original ability but different study time.
y-m-58-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Your design make clear 'who choose study time'?
y-m-58-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You write how to reduce other factors (like original ability)?
y-m-58-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You think about real-life difficulties or ethical issues too?
y-m-58-10.s.s2.model.0: Randomly divide students with similar ability into 2 groups; ask one group to study fixed time every day, while the other study as usual, then compare scores. Random division mix original ability evenly across both groups.
y-m-58-10.s.s2.model.1: Pair students with similar earlier diagnostic scores; ask one from each pair to increase study time and other study normally, then compare score differences.

y-m-58-08.title: When the vertex is not the minimum
y-m-58-08.topic: Quadratic-function basics: minimum on a restricted range
y-m-58-08.goal: Know that with a restricted domain a function minimum can occur at an interval endpoint instead of the vertex; find and fix the error, then make intervals meeting a condition.
y-m-58-08.material: Consider f(x)=(x−2)². Graph vertex is (2,0), opens upward (farther x is from 2, larger f(x) gets). If domain is closed interval [a,b] instead of all reals, find maximum and minimum. Figures: 2 2 0 2.
y-m-58-08.thinking.1: Judge while checking the range condition
y-m-58-08.thinking.2: Find all intervals meeting a constraint
y-m-58-08.prereq.0: Assume you know graph y=(x−p)² (vertex, symmetry, opens upward)
y-m-58-08.s.s1.prompt: Here is a solution when domain is 3≤x≤5. Choose the wrong line.
y-m-58-08.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether vertex x-coordinate 2 is inside interval 3≤x≤5.
y-m-58-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find the smallest of the values in line 2.
y-m-58-08.s.s1.line.0: Graph f(x)=(x−2)² is an upward-opening parabola with vertex (2,0). Figures: 2 2 0.
y-m-58-08.s.s1.line.2: Vertex y-coordinate is 0, so the minimum in this interval is also 0.
y-m-58-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 na mistake. Vertex x-coordinate 2 no dey inside interval 3 ≤ x ≤ 5. So minimum na f(3)=1, at x=3, the interval point nearest to 2.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose all intervals wey make minimum of f be 0 when domain na that interval.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.hint.0: First find x value wey make f(x)=0.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether each interval include that x value.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.r.a: You fit only check interval width or some values and forget to check whether vertex dey inside interval.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.r.b: This choice know say both interval endpoints dey included in domain too.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.r.c: You fit think minimum na 0 even though vertex outside interval.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.r.d: This choice check case where vertex dey inside interval.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.r.e: This choice know say vertex dey included even when e dey at interval endpoint.
y-m-58-08.s.s2.explain: For minimum to be 0, x=2, where f(x)=0, gats dey inside interval. 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 1 ≤ x ≤ 4, and 2 ≤ x ≤ 2.5 include 2; but −2 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 3 ≤ x ≤ 6 no include am.
y-m-58-08.s.s3.prompt: Choose integers a,b (a<b) to set interval [a,b], then find and enter every interval where minimum of f there na 1 and maximum na 9. (2 different intervals)
y-m-58-08.s.s3.hint.0: Find x values wey give maximum 9 from (x−2)²=9, then try put one at interval endpoint.
y-m-58-08.s.s3.hint.1: Check what minimum become if interval include x=2.
y-m-58-08.s.s3.fail.c1: a and b gats be integers with a<b.
y-m-58-08.s.s3.fail.c2: Maximum for this interval no be 9.
y-m-58-08.s.s3.fail.c3: Minimum for this interval no be 1. If vertex x=2 inside interval, minimum na 0.
y-m-58-08.s.s3.explain: Maximum 9 happen where x dey 3 away from 2 (−1 or 5), and minimum 1 happen where x dey 1 away from 2 (1 or 3). If interval contain vertex 2, minimum become 0, so only possible intervals na [3, 5] and [−1, 1].

y-m-58-01.title: For correspondence to be 'function'

y-m-58-01.goal: Apply two conditions 'every domain element get matched (nobody left out), and exactly one result' and codomain range to actual correspondences; judge dem, then make expression wey follow those conditions yourself.
y-m-58-01.material: For class, dem define function this way: 'When every element x of set X match with exactly one element of set Y, dem call correspondence a function from X to Y.' Today X={1, 2, 3, 4} and Y={0, 1, 2, 3}. Four correspondences, (가) to (라), dey.

y-m-58-07.title: Same data, different impression from a graph
y-m-58-07.topic: Showing data: same data, different graphs
y-m-58-07.goal: Understand that the vertical-axis start and range can change how the same data look; fix an exaggerated interpretation and choose a scale that meets a condition.
y-m-58-07.material: Made-up monthly shop sales: Jan 200, Feb 204, Mar 208, Apr 212 items. Article A line graph uses vertical axis 0-250; article B uses 198-214. Both graph the same points, but B's line looks steep.
y-m-58-07.thinking.0: Separate graph appearance from the data
y-m-58-07.thinking.2: Choose an axis that meets a condition
y-m-58-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all true statements about the two graphs.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.hint.0: Read January and April values on each graph and compare them.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think how the different vertical-axis ranges affect the line's apparent slope.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.o.a: Graph B looks steeper, so sales actually grew faster in B
y-m-58-07.s.s1.r.a: You read graph shape as a difference in the data.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.o.b: Changing the vertical-axis start and spacing can change the impression of the same data
y-m-58-07.s.s1.r.b: You know that display can change the impression even with the same data.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.o.c: Graph B starts its vertical axis above 0, so it falsifies the data values
y-m-58-07.s.s1.r.c: Graph B points still show the actual values. The issue is the impression created by its scale.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.o.d: Both graphs show equal sales values
y-m-58-07.s.s1.r.d: This choice confirms that the same data were drawn with different scales.
y-m-58-07.s.s1.explain: Both graphs show the same data and differ only in vertical axis. Changing the axis can make the line look steeper, but the sales themselves are equal. Starting at 0 is not always best either, such as when small changes matter.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose the wrong line in reporter B's explanation.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.hint.0: Read which value on graph B corresponds to height 0.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find the ratio of January sales to April sales yourself.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.line.0: Sales rose by 4 items each month: 200, 204, 208, 212.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.line.1: From January to April it rose by 12, which is 6 percent of the starting value.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.line.2: On graph B, April's point is 7 times higher than January's, so sales became 7 times as large.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.line.3: Therefore we can say this shop is growing very fast.
y-m-58-07.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. Graph B's vertical axis starts at 198, so each point's height shows only its difference from 198 (2 and 14). Actual sales rose from 200 to 212, which is 6 percent, not 7 times. Line 4's conclusion relies on this error.
